issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s decision is perverse and unreasonable and rests on conclusions that cannot legitimately be drawn from the proved facts.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding the prosecution case doubtful.
The High Court reversed the acquittal, finding that the trial court had rejected important evidence and circumstances on speculative grounds.
The Supreme Court found that the trial court’s reasons were unsound and against the weight of the evidence, and that the prosecution had established the case against the accused.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and its reversal was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal from an acquittal, reversal is justified where the trial judgment is perverse and unreasonable and rests on conclusions or inferences that cannot legitimately be drawn from the proved facts. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal in a criminal case in which an acquittal is under challenge.
predicates.high_court_reversed_acquittal: The High Court set aside the trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_findings_perverse: The trial court rejected important evidence or circumstances on speculative and unreasonable grounds.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the High Court has reversed it, and the trial court’s findings and inferences are perverse and unsupported by the proved facts, the reversal of the acquittal is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: An accused may be convicted for murder and related offences where the evidence establishes participation in an unlawful assembly with the relevant common object and proves the assaults and resulting injuries.
material_facts: The prosecution eyewitnesses identified the accused and described their assaults on the deceased and other people, the abduction of another person, and the removal of the bodies.
The Supreme Court found that the testimony of the eyewitnesses was credible and was corroborated by medical evidence concerning the injuries.
The evidence established motive arising from prior hostility, the presence of light at the scene, and circumstances connecting an accused’s recovered firearm with cartridges found there.
The Supreme Court found that the accused shared the relevant common object and upheld their convictions under Sections 302/149 and the other offences for which they had been convicted.
issues.conclusion: The convictions and sentences were upheld, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code supports liability for an offence committed by a member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object. Applying that provision, the Court upheld the convictions under Sections 302/149, 147, 148, 323/149, 324/149, 307/149, 364/149 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code on the evidence of the assaults, the eyewitnesses, and the medical corroboration. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this ruling.
